s1-core.deltaSummaryMarkdown:
Inspected the reworked `nesting.rs` (cost units per construct, the regex group cap, TypeScript postfix `!`, the fail-closed coarse bound with its short-source fast path) and the step-budget minimum in `engine.rs`, `mod.rs` and `token_resolution.rs`, plus the new tests named in each finding.

I rebuilt the throwaway probe under `artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/probe` and probed with it:
- every earlier crash case and new bypass attempts, in release on an 8 MiB thread;
- a binary search of the deepest accepted source for 53 constructs, in debug on a 1 MiB thread;
- the step-budget-0 sweep.

No input crashed or hung. I relied on the coordinator's passing check evidence and reran no test group.

S1-F1 and S1-F9 are resolved; S1-F2..F8 stay resolved. No findings remain open.

Residual note, not a finding: the accepted depths are calibrated for unoptimized code on a 1 MiB stack, so hosts resolving on much smaller threads keep less margin. The `stack_limit` doc already warns to leave room on the resolving thread's stack, and wasm32 is sprint 2's PLT-2.
s1-core.summaryMarkdown: EXP-1, PLT-1, EVAL-1..3 and EVAL-5 hold in source and tests (snapshot/type order, inputs through `resolve_value` at `Position::Unchecked` with cycle detection, integral/rounding/depth/node rules, dependency collection of inputs, export round trip); memory, stack and step trips are uncatchable as tested, Atomics cannot block, ReDoS stops at the step budget. The sprint fails on four major defects found by probes: oxc stack overflow aborts the host on deeply nested expression text (S1-F1), unfrozen shared intrinsics (tamed members, Promise, iterator helpers) let expressions affect each other (S1-F2), the step budget depends on prior evaluations through QuickJS's interrupt counter (S1-F3), and QuickJS-only syntax errors lack positions (S1-F4); plus four minor ones (S1-F5..F8).

s2-platforms.summaryMarkdown: PLT-2 and PLT-3 are met as worded. I reran `expressions_wasm` (4/4 under `wasm-bindgen-test-runner` 0.2.129, Node 24, Homebrew LLVM) after the S2-F1 repair. The test module's 52 imports are all wasm-bindgen's. `__stack_pointer` starts at 1 MiB (the default stack). The private in-crate clock matches the shim's `double(void)` and is no longer public API. A throwaway wasm probe ran the deepest source each nesting construct accepts on the default stack: all 18 return without trapping. CI keeps the matrix's `--all-features` clippy/test and the default wasm32 check. The new Ubuntu job installs `clang`/`llvm` (`/usr/bin/clang`, `/usr/bin/llvm-ar`), installs the locked `wasm-bindgen-cli` exactly, and runs the feature check and the group. S2-F2's consumer-facing documentation is now a recorded `t16-docs` obligation. Residual risk only GitHub can settle: Ubuntu's clang 18, and MSVC (`/std:c11 /experimental:c11atomics`, aarch64-calibrated nesting weights on an x86_64 1 MiB thread).

s3-modules.deltaSummaryMarkdown: Inspected the repair delta in `engine.rs` (`load_modules`, `connect`/`visit` iterative Tarjan with `Components`, `evaluate_component`, `thrower`, `module_error`, `module_table` seeding `ModuleEntry::compiled`) and `modules.rs` (`document_modules` rooted at token `imports`, `walk` with `Next::Specifier`/`Next::Module` following bare specifiers through reached host modules, `DocumentModules::compiled`), plus the new tests `an_import_cycle_evaluates_in_es_module_order`, `module_errors_name_the_module_that_threw`, `modules_outside_a_cycle_have_their_own_step_budget`, `a_host_module_nothing_imports_requests_no_document_module` and `document_cycles_name_the_module_that_threw`. Tarjan emits components dependencies-first and leads each by its lowest-index (first-reached) member; RefCell borrows are released before QuickJS declare/eval. Re-ran the original probes against the repaired code: cycle order is now `b,a` (matches Node), the TDZ case reports `module \`b\`: ReferenceError: a is not initialized at line 3, column 22` (matches Node), document cycle `a.js` throwing reports `a.js`/`a` with line 5, outside dependency `c.js` reports `c.js`/`./c.js` with line 2, the cycle-plus-dependency budget shape that previously exceeded `expression steps` now passes, an unreached host module importing a declared specifier yields `Ready` with no requests, and a reached host -> host -> document chain still requests `doc.js`. Sprint checks `check-expr-modules` and `check-expr-document-modules` passed (executed 2). Note, not a defect: a missing-export link error inside a cycle has no stack frame and is attributed to the cycle leader, which is the exporting module the QuickJS message names, consistent with MOD-3's wording.
s3-modules.summaryMarkdown: EXP-3 declaration validation and later-declaration-replaces-earlier, the kinded catalog (atomic `provide_module`/`provide_requested_module`/`replace_module`, kind mismatch both ways, invalid ids, `provide_json_batch` over a module id, `remove_document`), discovery rejecting a module where JSON is expected, request rounds through relative imports, language by extension, `resolve`/previews/`validate_complete` across contexts, deterministic request order, MOD-4 via both routes, and MOD-3 identities for acyclic modules all hold in source, tests and probes. Two major defects remain: cycle evaluation order and error/budget attribution in cycles (S3-F1, MOD-1/MOD-3), and document-module requests caused by unreached host modules (S3-F2, MOD-2); plus a minor double-compilation issue (S3-F3). Imports of the built-in `dxn.dtcg` modules (part of MOD-1) cannot exist before s4-native and are left to that sprint and the final review. Memory rules (I/O-free catalog, atomic mutations, consumer-neutral wording, `dxn.dtcg.*` ids) are respected.

s4-native.summaryMarkdown:
**Verdict: passed** (full re-review of plan revision 5). All 8 findings are resolved, and the repairs were checked by independent probes as well as the new tests.

**Color API (NAT-2)**
- Conversions still match colorjs.io 0.7.1 to 3.7e-12 across 1,680 components.
- Mixes with white, black or gray now take the other color's hue in oklch, lch, hsl and hwb, and match colorjs exactly.
- The gamut test runs on linear light, so shared primaries count as in gamut.
- Boundary colors round-trip within 1e-9.
- Non-finite inputs give valid colors.

**Native modules and the macro (NAT-3, NAT-4, NAT-5)**
- Export names are validated in both the builder (panic) and the macro (compile error), so the declarations parse for every accepted name.
- All 12 value models (de)serialize as validated DTCG JSON and map to their TypeScript names.
- `Json<T>` covers any other serializable return.
- Built-in TypeErrors carry one prefix.

**Unchanged since the first review:** the bridge sandbox (the bridge is unreachable, exports and constants are frozen, setup leaves no global) and MOD-5.

**Residual, noted under S4-F3:** an A98 RGB component below about 4e-7, or a Rec. 2020 component below about 1.5e-6, now reads as 0. That breaks the literal 1e-9 round-trip bound by at most that amount, and is documented only on a private constant. The owner may want to state it on `Color::convert` or in the NAT-2 wording.

s5-finish.deltaSummaryMarkdown: Criteria unchanged (PLT-4, DOC-1). The delta since the previous reattestation is the `DtcgError::Expression` row of the errors table in `docs/11-errors-limits-and-diagnostics.md`, which now reads "with the authored line and column when QuickJS reports one", matching `caught_message`/`frame_position` in `expressions/engine.rs`. A search of `docs/`, the README and the website finds no remaining unconditional position claim. S5-F1, S5-F2, S5-F3 and S5-F5 stay resolved as reattested before; `check --sprint s5-finish` passed 3/3 on this snapshot.
s5-finish.summaryMarkdown: PLT-4 passes: `tests/expressions_wasm.rs` adds a TypeScript host-module import (`step(4, 2)` = 9), a host native module call (`double(21)` = 42 and the caught `brand/native.divide: division by zero`) and a `dxn.dtcg/color` OKLCH conversion asserting colorjs.io's reference values rounded to six places, matching `expressions_modules`, `expressions_native` and `expressions_color`; the s5 `check-expr-wasm` run recorded 7 passing tests. DOC-1 coverage is complete (new chapter included under `cfg(feature = "expressions")` inside the doctest module with 7 passing doctests, every listed chapter and website page updated, the new page has title/description/order 135 and all relative links and anchors resolve, the S2-F2 clock statement is in chapter 15 and platforms, wording is consumer-free, forbidden paths untouched, all `documentation` doctests pass with `--all-features`). Most claims match source (limits and defaults, reserved namespace, export-name validation, `Json<T>`/`NativeReturn`, built-ins and their messages, color API and the new precision note, CI jobs, `wasm-bindgen` 0.2.129). Five minor accuracy defects remain (S5-F1 to S5-F5), so DOC-1 fails until they are repaired.

s6-final-repair.summaryMarkdown: Full re-review against the amended criteria; all six findings are resolved and the earlier evidence was rerun (catch/finally forms, positions, name collisions, cycles, TS, documents, freezing). SBX-3/EVAL-5 dispositions match the owner's option-A decision; the later widening (S6-F2) is recorded in SBX-4/EVAL-6 and t21, and the disposition text predates it. SBX-4/EVAL-6 hold as amended: no channel remains outside the owner's exception in the probes, stack overflows (calls and the regexp compiler) are uncatchable, and the docs match observed behavior. Known, documented residue: `Object.create` of an object nothing inherited from at freeze time stays read-only; a self-made `RangeError`/`SyntaxError` with QuickJS's overflow message is reported as a stack overflow (deterministic).

s7-final-repair-2.summaryMarkdown:
Passed (fourth pass).

**Findings:** S7-F1 to S7-F8 are all resolved: S7-F3 by the owner's option A (SBX-5 supersedes SBX-2), S7-F8 by passing redeclared parameters through.

**Disposition:** `criterion:SBX-2` (superseded, decided by the owner) matches the recorded decision. SBX-5 repeats SBX-2 in full plus the precisely named exception, and t26 owns it with the stack/sandbox/async-overflow groups.

**Behavior re-probed** (`artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/s7-probe` `cases1` to `cases10`, against HEAD via `s7-probe-head`):
- Overflows fail in async bodies, async parameters, every syntactic `return` close, wrapped errors and uncaught `SuppressedError`. The only non-failures are the excepted `return` forms and deterministic outcomes (the pattern-nesting `SyntaxError`, `then` callbacks that never run).
- RegExp compatibility matches HEAD. Module names are digests. The color and non-finite-argument repairs hold.
- Docs describe the mechanisms and the exception accurately.

s8-final-repair-3.summaryMarkdown:
Passed.

**E3-F1 is repaired.**
- `FREEZE_SOURCE` `isOverflow` walks `SuppressedError`/`AggregateError` with no count cap. It visits each object once (a `WeakSet`) and reads only data properties.
- `check`, the rejection tracker and `note_overflow` all use it. The Rust side calls it through the saved `Persistent`; the old Rust walk and its 1,000 cap are gone.
- `f3-probe/cases1.json` now fails with the stack overflow in all 21 cases: 100 to 12,000 callbacks, overflow first or last, sync, async and the recursive variant. It previously caught or swallowed the overflow from about 1,000 callbacks on.
- The new test `a_stack_overflow_wrapped_however_deeply_is_still_one` covers the same shapes.

**Requested probes** (`artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/s7-probe`, `cases11.json` to `cases13.json`; the runner gained `steps` and a follow-up token):
- Cyclic and self-referential wrappers terminate: a `SuppressedError` whose `error`/`suppressed` is itself, an `AggregateError` containing itself, mutual cycles, and an `errors` array that contains itself. Without an overflow they are ordinary catchable errors or rejections; with an engine overflow inside they fail as a stack overflow, sync and async.
- A sparse `errors.length = 2**32-1` fails deterministically with `LimitExceeded { kind: "expression steps" }`, in a catch, a rejection and uncaught.
- A walk that exhausts a 50-step budget inside the rejection tracker fails with the step limit; building the same array alone fits the budget. A larger one fails with the memory limit.
- An evaluation already tripped by recursion still reports a stack overflow after a later rejection.
- Near the stack limit (call depth 150 to 259, one step at a time; plain recursion fits up to 246), async, async-wrapped and sync-wrapped overflows fail as overflows at every depth.

Observation, not a finding: when the tracker's call into `isOverflow` fails, `is_stack_overflow` returns `false` and leaves the exception pending. Every failure mode I could produce (steps, memory, a tripped guard) still ends the evaluation with the right limit.

findings.descriptionMarkdown: Resolved for expression calls. The retry after a drain is sound: with a carried counter the evaluation can only reach as many or more interrupt checks than with a fresh one, so a pass with a carried counter implies a pass with a fresh one, and a failure is re-run from a full counter. I swept step budgets 0 and 1 against iteration counts 100–15,000, with and without a preceding token: the outcome matched the token evaluated alone in every case except one. That exception is the step-budget-0 compile path, recorded as S1-F9.

Resolved. `"1), (2"` and the top-level `await`/`export` injection both fail with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token at line 1, column 2`. `check_expression` parses the authored text alone, as exactly one expression running to the end of input.
Resolved. `a²` now fails with `` `inputs`: `a²` is not a JavaScript identifier ``. Validation uses oxc's `is_identifier_start` and `is_identifier_part`.

Resolved. The diagnostic message keeps only a kind and the authored position: an error class (only when it is ASCII alphanumeric and ends in `Error`) or one of the fixed categories. Thrown values and source quotes are dropped. A user-defined error class name still passes through; it is an authored identifier, which is acceptable.

Resolved. `with_stack_limit(0)` now evaluates (`"ok"`), because values below 16 KiB count as 16 KiB. The doc of `ExpressionOptions::stack_limit` states that the limit must leave room on the resolving thread's stack, and that a limit near that stack's size aborts the process.

Resolved. A budget of 0 now counts as 1, in `Session::new` and in the reported `LimitExceeded` limit. My probe (`a` with 4,996 iterations, then `b` with none, at `with_step_budget(0)`) now passes. I swept `a` from 9,900 to 9,998 iterations: whenever `a` passes alone, `a` then `b` also passes, and the first failures (9,998 and above) come from `a` itself exceeding the budget.

Resolved. `__rquickjs_host_now_us` is no longer `pub`; it keeps `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` and the wasm32-unknown-unknown cfg and sits after the `use` block. The wasm group passes (4/4), the test module's 52 imports are all wasm-bindgen's, and wasm32 rustdoc of `dxn_dtcg::expressions` no longer shows the item.

Resolved for this sprint. The clock's doc comment states the module-wide effect, and `t16-docs` now requires the wasm32 section of `docs/15-expressions.md` and the website's `platforms` page to state it for consumers: the crate defines `__rquickjs_host_now_us` as 0 for the whole module, other `quickjs-jit` users read that clock, and they cannot supply or redefine it. The s5 and final reviews check the published text.

Import cycles were evaluated in non-standard order, cycle errors named the entry module instead of the thrower, and acyclic dependencies of a cycle shared its budget. Resolved: Tarjan components evaluated dependencies-first and entered at the first-reached member; failures attributed to the innermost table-module stack frame with that module's position mapping; verified by tests and probes.

An unreached host module importing a declared specifier caused a document-module request. Resolved: the walk starts at token `imports` specifiers and follows only host modules it reaches; verified by test and probe (unreached: Ready, no requests; reached host -> host -> document: requested).

Modules were compiled twice per resolution. Resolved: `walk` returns every compiled module keyed by its session name (`DocumentModules::compiled`) and `module_table` seeds `ModuleEntry::compiled`, so reached host and document modules compile once per resolution; unreached host modules are not compiled. Verified by source inspection; covered behaviorally by the existing groups.

**Mixing in a cylindrical space ignores powerless hues.**

Expected (CSS Color 4 §12.4, and colorjs.io 0.7.1, the source of the epic's reference values): when an endpoint is achromatic in the interpolation space (OKLCH/LCH chroma about 0, HSL saturation 0, HWB whiteness + blackness >= 100), its hue counts as missing and the other color's hue is used. For example `mix(white, blue, 0.5)` in OKLCH is `oklch(0.72601, 0.15661, 264.052)`, or `#74a3ff`; black + red in OKLCH keeps hue 29.234 (`#630000`); white + blue in HSL is `[240, 50, 75]`.

Observed: `Color::convert` gives white an OKLCH hue of 180 (from `atan2` of rounding noise), so `Color::mix(white, blue, 0.5)` returns hue 222.026, which is `#00baec` (cyan). Black + red returns hue 14.617 (`#62001c`), and HSL white + blue returns `[270, 75, 75]`. `dxn.dtcg/color` `mix` returns the same values (`toHex(mix(white, blue))` is `#00baec`). Tinting and shading, the most common uses of mixing, produce visibly wrong hues. The tests mix only chromatic endpoints, so they do not catch this.

Repair: in `Color::mix_in`, treat the hue of an endpoint that is achromatic in `space` as missing and use the other endpoint's hue (0 when both are achromatic). Use thresholds like colorjs's. Also write powerless hues as 0 in conversion output so that grays convert deterministically. Add cases to `tests/color_conversion.rs` against colorjs references: white, black and gray mixed with chromatic colors in oklch, lch, hsl and hwb. Add one such case through `dxn.dtcg/color` `mix` in `tests/expressions_color.rs`.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified against colorjs.io 0.7.1. White + blue gives `#74a3ff` in oklch, `#af89ff` in lch, `[240,50,75]` in hsl and `[240,50,0]` in hwb. Black + red and gray + red (0.25) also match in all four spaces.

**`in_gamut` reports in-gamut colors as out of gamut on a shared primary or a gamut boundary.**

Expected: sRGB red `[1,0,0]` and blue `[0,0,1]` lie in the A98 RGB gamut, because A98 RGB shares sRGB's red and blue primaries (colorjs `inGamut('a98rgb')` returns true). A color that lies exactly on an RGB space's boundary is in that space's gamut.

Observed: `srgb(1,0,0).in_gamut(A98Rgb)` and `srgb(0,0,1).in_gamut(A98Rgb)` return `false`. So does `Color::new(A98Rgb, [1,0,0]).convert(Srgb).in_gamut(A98Rgb)`, and `inGamut({srgb red}, 'a98-rgb')` in `dxn.dtcg/color`. The cause: the test runs on encoded coordinates. The pure power transfer function (exponent 1/2.2) turns linear rounding noise of about -1e-17 into about -1e-8, which is outside the 1e-9 tolerance. Rec. 2020 has the same pure-power transfer, so its boundary colors are exposed in the same way.

Repair: test the gamut on linear-light coordinates (`multiply(XYZ_TO_*, xyz)`, before encoding) with the 1e-9 tolerance. Every transfer function is monotonic and maps 0 and 1 to themselves, so the result is the same as testing the encoded coordinates without the noise amplification. Add tests: the sRGB primaries, secondaries and white are in the gamut of `display-p3`, `a98-rgb`, `prophoto-rgb` and `rec2020`, and every RGB space's own primaries remain in its gamut after a round trip through each other space.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. `in_gamut` now tests linear light. sRGB red, blue, white and black are in the gamut of a98-rgb, rec2020, display-p3, prophoto-rgb, hsl and hwb. Display P3 green is outside the sRGB and HSL gamuts.

**The criterion's 1e-9 round-trip bound does not hold on gamut boundaries, and the test hides how large the error is there.**

Expected: NAT-2 says that in-gamut round trips through every space return the input within 1e-9, with no exception for boundary colors.

Observed: the test uses only interior colors. Its comment gives the boundary error as about 1e-8. Measured: `a98-rgb [1,0,0]` through `oklch` comes back with g = 1.02e-7, and `rec2020 [0,1,0]` through `oklch` comes back with b = 4.19e-7. Reviewer judgement: the error is inherent to f64 arithmetic with pure power transfer functions. colorjs itself gives 8.15e-9 for sRGB red in A98. Restricting the 1e-9 bound to interior colors is therefore an acceptable reading only if the criterion says so and the boundary behaviour is pinned by a test.

Repair: the coordinator amends NAT-2 (with the owner's agreement) to state the 1e-9 bound for colors inside every RGB gamut and an explicit looser bound for boundary colors, for example 1e-6. Add a test that holds every RGB space's primaries and secondaries to that bound through every space. Correct the magnitude in the test comment, and note the limitation in the `Color::convert` docs.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. Every primary, secondary, white and black of each RGB space, and sRGB boundary colors expressed in all 14 spaces, now round-trip within 1e-9 through every space in whose gamut they lie. A residual remains: an A98 RGB component in (0, about 4e-7), or a Rec. 2020 component in (0, about 1.5e-6), now encodes as 0. For example a98 `[0.3, 1e-7, 0.6]` returns g = 0, an error of 1e-7. Some band near 0 must fail at f64 precision with a pure power curve, so the reviewer accepts this as meeting NAT-2 in substance. The band is documented only on the private `NOISE` constant.

**Export names that are reserved words, or not identifiers, produce invalid declarations, and `default` silently becomes the module's default export.**

Expected: NAT-5 requires the declarations to parse without diagnostics for every registered native module. NAT-4 requires a clear compile error for misuse.

Observed:
- `#[expression_module]` on `pub fn new(value: f64)` renders `export const new: (value: number) => number;`. oxc reports "'new' is a reserved word". `new` is a common Rust function name; `delete` and `default` fail the same way.
- `NativeModule::new(..).function("my-fn", ..)` renders `export const my-fn: …`, which also fails to parse.
- At run time the wrapper still exports these names (`Object.keys` gives `default,delete,new`). `default` becomes the namespace's `default` export.

`every_declared_export_exists_at_run_time` cannot see any of this, because its fixtures use only identifier names.

Repair, either of:
- (a) Validate export names. In the macro, an exported name that is not a JS IdentifierName usable as a binding (a reserved word, `default`, or a non-identifier) is a compile error that points to `#[expression(name = "…")]`. For builder registrations, return a `DtcgError::Expression` that names the module and the export when the session starts, or panic as documented in `function`/`constant`.
- (b) Render every export as `const __export_n: T; export { __export_n as "name" };` inside `declare module`, and still reject `default`.

Add a trybuild case for `pub fn new`, and a declarations test whose modules use such names.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. The builder panics with a documented message for `new`, `default`, `delete`, `my-fn`, the empty name and `1a`. The macro reports a compile error (trybuild cases `reserved_name`, `invalid_name`). Declarations for 41 TypeScript contextual keywords and other edge names (`type`, `declare`, `module`, `async`, `constructor`, `__proto__`, `satisfies`, …) parse without oxc diagnostics, and all 41 plus a `Json` export are callable at run time. The runtime and macro reserved-word lists are identical.

**Only 4 of the `dxn_dtcg::values` models can be used as native function types.**

Expected: NAT-4 maps `dxn_dtcg::values` models to their DTCG value type names, and NAT-3 lets closures take and return serde types. The declarations (d-declarations) declare `Shadow`, `Typography`, `Border`, `Transition`, `Gradient`, `StrokeStyle`, `FontFamily` and `FontWeight` to editors.

Observed: `Serialize`/`Deserialize` (`serde_with_json!`), `NativeReturn` (`plain_returns!`) and the macro's `VALUE_MODELS` cover only `Color`, `Dimension`, `Duration` and `CubicBezier`. A host function such as `pub fn soften(shadow: Shadow) -> Shadow` does not compile, and if it did, its signature would map to `unknown`, although editors see a declared `Shadow` type.

Repair: give each remaining DTCG 2025.10 model a DTCG JSON `to_json` and a validated serde implementation, as the four existing ones have. Add them to `plain_returns!` and `VALUE_MODELS`. Cover a composite model (a shadow and a typography value) in `tests/expressions_native_macro.rs`. Alternatively, the coordinator records an owner-approved amendment that limits NAT-4 to the four models.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. A macro module taking and returning Shadow (one layer and an array of layers), Typography, Border (with a dash array), Gradient, Transition, StrokeStyle, FontFamily and FontWeight round-trips through expressions. Its declarations use the DTCG type names and parse cleanly, and an invalid fontWeight throws a TypeError.

**Plain returns accept only a fixed list of types, while the docs say any serializable value.**

Expected: NAT-3 says closures return serde-serializable types. The doc of `NativeModule::function` says the closure returns "a serializable value, or `Result<T, E>`".

Observed: a closure that returns a host `#[derive(Serialize)]` struct (for example `|p: Pair| Pair { .. }`) does not compile. It needs `Ok::<_, Infallible>(…)` (the test `swap` does this). Plain returns are limited to the primitives, `String`, `Value`, `Vec`, `Option`, `[T; N]`, `BTreeMap<String, T>` and the four models. A blanket implementation would overlap with the `Result` implementation, so this is a coherence limit rather than an oversight.

Repair: add a public wrapper (for example `expressions::Json<T: Serialize>` implementing `NativeReturn`), or document exactly which types are accepted as plain returns and show the `Ok::<_, Infallible>` form in a doctest. In either case, ask the coordinator to align the NAT-3 wording. The macro already wraps plain returns, so it is not affected.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. `Json<T>` is public, and a closure returning `Json(P { a })` works from expressions. The `.function` docs list the supported returns.

**Built-in `TypeError` messages repeat the function name.**

Expected: a single prefix that names the function, for example `dxn.dtcg.px: argument 1 must be a number`.

Observed: `dxn.dtcg.px: px: argument 1 must be a number` and `dxn.dtcg.dimension: dimension: unit `em` is not one of px, rem`. The bridge prefixes `<specifier>.<name>:`, and `builtins::type_error` adds `<name>:` again. The same happens in `dxn.dtcg/color`.

Repair: remove the function-name prefix from `builtins::type_error`, and make `tests/expressions_builtin.rs` and `tests/expressions_color.rs` assert the full message after the prefix.

**Re-review (snapshot b96986cc):** Verified. `builtins::type_error` adds no inner prefix. The tests assert full messages such as `dxn.dtcg/color.mix: argument 2 is not a valid color: …`.

**The Rust color API returns invalid DTCG colors for non-finite inputs.**

Expected: NAT-2 says results are valid DTCG colors.

Observed:
- `red.lighten(f64::NAN)` serializes as `components: [null, null, null]`.
- `red.mix(&blue, f64::NAN)` gives null components and a null `alpha`.
- `red.with_alpha(f64::NAN)` gives `alpha: null`.
- `Color::new` accepts out-of-range or NaN components unchecked, and `to_json`/`Serialize` then emit invalid DTCG JSON.

The JavaScript bridge avoids most of these cases, because `JSON.stringify` turns NaN into null and the builtins reject null. A host that calls the public Rust API, or a native function that returns a `Color`, does not get that protection.

Repair: handle non-finite amounts and alpha in `mix_in`, `lighten`/`darken` and `with_alpha`, either by treating NaN as no change and clamping infinities, or by documenting a panic. Document that `Color::new` does not validate, or have it clamp into range, and add unit tests in `tests/color_conversion.rs`.

**The async-body wrap rejects valid JavaScript: an async function or arrow whose body declares a `var` and a function of the same name, or the same function twice, now fails to compile.**

Expected: instrumentation only inserts text and keeps every valid program valid with the same meaning (`compile.rs` `instrument`: "Only text is inserted"). Observed: `instrument` moves the whole body of every async function into a block (`{ try { ... } catch (x) { ... } }`). Inside a block a function declaration is lexical, so it now collides with a `var` of the same name or with a second declaration. Probe `artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/s7-probe` (`cases2.json`, release, `opt-level = 3`; same cases against HEAD with `s7-probe-head`):

- `async () => { var g = 1; function g() {} ... }`: the same error.
- `(async function () { function g() { return 1 } function g() { return 2 } r = g(); })()` gives `SyntaxError: invalid redefinition of lexical identifier` (HEAD: `2`).
The same happens in host and document modules, the bundled single-file libraries hosts are expected to provide, and in TypeScript (its output is re-instrumented). A module that worked before this sprint can now fail to load.

Add the cases above to `tests/expressions_async_overflow.rs` (expressions and a host module) as must-compile, must-evaluate cases.

Original finding:

**The new `return`-method wrap changes the meaning of a valid body: a `var` that redeclares a parameter now shadows it with `undefined`.**

Expected: instrumentation only inserts text and keeps every valid program's meaning (the lesson of S7-F1, now applied to `return` methods).

Observed: `instrument` moves a `return` method's body into an arrow (`{ return checked(() => { ... }); }`). The arrow has no parameters, so a body `var x` declares a new binding in the arrow instead of naming the parameter (`artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/s7-probe`, `cases8.json`, compared with HEAD via `s7-probe-head`):
- `const o = { return(x) { var x; return x; } }; o.return(5)` returns `undefined` (HEAD: `5`).
- `return(x = 1) { var x; return x; }` called with 5 returns `undefined` (HEAD: `5`).
A `return: (x) => { var x; ... }` arrow has the same problem. Redeclaring parameters with `var` is legal and occurs in transpiled and minified code, including iterator helpers in polyfills, which is the code that defines `return(value)` methods. `this`, `arguments`, `super`, `new.target`, hoisting and expression bodies are preserved (`cases8.json` `sem-*`), and `iterator_return_methods_keep_their_meaning` does not cover parameter redeclaration.

Repair: keep the body's bindings, for example by passing every bound name of the parameters through the arrow (`return checked((x) => { var x; ... }, x)`, including destructured names), or by wrapping the method value instead of its body. Add `var`-redeclares-parameter cases (simple and default parameters, method and arrow forms) to `iterator_return_methods_keep_their_meaning`.

**The overflow check stops unwrapping wrapped errors after a fixed number of values, so a stack overflow wrapped deeply enough in `SuppressedError`s is caught or discarded. This is outside the owner's iterator-close exception.**

Expected (SBX-5; docs/15 and website 'The sandbox and its limits': the internal check 'unwraps `SuppressedError` and `AggregateError`'): an overflow anywhere inside a wrapped error stops the evaluation, however the error is nested.

Observed: both unwrapping paths have fixed limits. `check` in `FREEZE_SOURCE` (`engine.rs`) stops after 10,000 values and walks depth-first (it pushes `error` then `suppressed`, so it follows the `suppressed` chain first). `is_stack_overflow` in Rust, used by the rejection tracker and for uncaught errors, gives up after 1,000 values. `DisposableStack.prototype.dispose` builds one nested `SuppressedError` per throwing callback, so expression code can push the overflow past either limit. Probe `artifacts-temp/agentx/dtcg-expressions/f3-probe` (release, `opt-level = 3` for quickjs-jit-sys; `f3probe cases1.json`): with a few thousand throwing callbacks around an engine-recursion overflow, a sync `try`/`catch` returns `caught SuppressedError` (`ds-first n=6000`, `ds-last n=12000`); in an async body the result is `swallowed` from about 1,000 callbacks (`ds-async-last n=1000`). With 100 callbacks every variant still fails as an overflow. Call recursion was always caught because its allocations cross the guard threshold.

Repair:
1. In `check` and `is_stack_overflow`, traverse `SuppressedError.error`/`.suppressed` and `AggregateError.errors` until the queue is empty, tracking visited objects (a `Set` in JS, raw object identity in Rust) instead of a fixed count, so cycles end and depth cannot hide an overflow. The JS loop already costs steps; the Rust loop is bounded by the objects the code itself allocated.
2. Add cases to `tests/expressions_async_overflow.rs`: a long `DisposableStack` chain with the overflow first and last, sync caught and in an async body, each failing as a stack overflow.
